utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters; good morning, counsel for the Prosecution and the Defence. I don't know which clock we are governed by. I see on the transcript it is 9.28. The clock in the courtroom shows 9.25. Anyway, this is just a remark to say that we ought to be governed by the same clock, and I don't know which one it should be. So we're going to resume our work continuing with the re-examination of Mr. Kvocka. Mr. Kvocka, let me remind you that you are continuing to testify under oath and you will be asked questions by your counsel. Mr. Simic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, we broke off yesterday when I asked you whether Mr. Bob Reid had asked you about Mr. Prcac. You answered yes. So, as advised by the President, let me say that on page 35 of your interview with Mr. Reid, the Serbian version, and 31 of the English, I think, you were asked whether, while you were in Omarska, Mr. Dragoljub Prcac was working with you in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that question was put to me and I said that he had not, and he didn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bob Reid went back to the person called Dragoljub Prcac on page 136 of the Serbian version, and in the English version, 128 and 129. He asked you, "Do you know a person by the name of Prcac?"

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He has been a long-standing employee in the public security station. Actually, he used to work there while it was called the SUP, the Secretariat for Internal Affairs. After the change in 1990, I don't think he continued working. He retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Reid, he asked you whether you knew that he worked in the investigations centre after you; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I remember saying that I didn't know, that we didn't meet there ever, but that I heard later that he had worked there. During the summer and autumn, in Prijedor, I heard that from someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: On the same page, Mr. Reid asked you whether you knew what his role was in the investigations centre; do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, and I remember answering that I didn't know. I know that he was a mobilised reserve policeman. That was the status he had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Prcac had worked in the police structure before the changes of 1990. Can you tell us whether you knew him as a policeman and what kind of reputation he had?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We met several times during the performance of our duties. When I started working in the police, he held the position of crime technician. In those days, as a policeman, if a criminal act had been committed and if an on-site inspection was required, I would secure the site until the inspection team arrived; I would also secure the activities of that team until the completion of their work. So he would usually be a member of the team consisting of the crime inspector, sometimes an investigating judge, and a crime technician, whose main task was to take photographs of the site, to take fingerprints, to make a sketch of the location, and so on. I know these things from theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kvocka, during yesterday's hearing I showed you a letter from Mr. Komarica, the Bishop of Banja Luka. I'm sorry, by the Bishop to Simo Drljaca, and on that occasion mention is made of the Honourable Stipo Sosic, the parish priest. Do you remember that name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it from yesterday, from the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, were you aware that the priest Stipo Sosic was detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this letter, it can be seen that he was arrested on the 15th of June, 1992, which need not necessarily imply that he arrived in Omarska on the same date. And as you know, from the 16th to the 19th, I was on sick leave, in fact, I was off, and when I came back, the only change I noticed was Jadranka Gavranovic, whom I knew well from the village of Omarska, who was detained there, and she told me that she, her unmarried husband Igor Kondic, also someone called Lujic, also called Lujo, had been arrested, that they had been accused of smuggling weapons, and that they had been put up there, and it was only her that I saw on that occasion. It was easy to notice her because I knew her well and she was among the women, the small group of women. As for these other two, Lujic and Igor, I only saw Igor when I visited my brothers-in-law, when he was covered in bruises, and this was on the 26th or the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where is Mrs. Jadranka from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, my learned friend showed you yesterday a document marked 3/189. So could we please go back to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Kvocka be shown this document 3/189, please. Could the usher place on the ELMO the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, would you please tell me the date when this document was compiled?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th of June, 1992. And the list of employees, monthly work results for the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, how many days does June have?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirty.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how can somebody compile a report while two working days of the month still remain, the month for which the report is being compiled?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That illustrates what I was saying yesterday. Two or three days don't mean anything in terms of salaries. So salaries are not prepared according to work schedules but simply to reflect the presence of the work throughout the month or not, but not whether he actually worked every day or not. So what is important here, if somebody retired halfway, in the middle of the month, or if he was on sick leave for ten days or more - I don't know the exact limit - then he receives his personal incomes in two parts. If somebody's away for two days upon permission of the commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We heard all about that yesterday. Mr. Kvocka, we spoke at length about your status after taking back your brothers-in-law on the 24th of June and after being removed from Omarska. It says the 24th of June. It should be the 23rd. I'm sorry. What was your position during those days? Did anyone tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first encounter with Dusko Jankovic ended by him saying, "Go home and wait." However, I found that rather vague. If he had immediately told me something more specific, then I would have something to hope for. But the way in which he expressed himself told me that this would be some kind of a suspension or even worse. So I couldn't -- I didn't know what to do. I called up the secretary. She would say, "Call back again." So I didn't know what kind of preparations had been made in advance should I appear. Then suddenly they said, as if it was a hasty decision, "Go to Tukovi on the 1st of July." However - I must say thanks to the Prosecution who produced the seized documents - I was able to establish exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Would you explain to Their Honours what you discovered on the basis of the documents that were seized during the investigations, which, I fear, deprived the Defence to have all the documents it needed to prepare its case properly, but we'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it was was a de facto suspension, and the next step could have been my total dismissal, and after that I could have been sent to the front and all the other problems that would follow. However, the chief of the security centre in Banja Luka, who is superior to the Public Security Station in Prijedor, sent a dispatch ordering -- a circular letter to all the police stations, including Prijedor, therefore, ordering that all employees who have not firmly decided who they were as Serbs and that they could be relied on and who have access to important information could not be dismissed as had been done in some cases. Apparently, this had already been done by someone somewhere. So by his order --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Chamber to be able to follow what we're talking about, could I ask the usher -- D 39/1, could that document be shown to the witness so he can refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, will you look at this document, please, though you have had occasion to see it among the documents disclosed to you. Do you have before you a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, adopted on the 22nd of June, 1992, registered under 03-531/92?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Would you please answer my questions. Is this a decision of the Crisis Staff of the 22nd of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Would you please carefully read out the first paragraph of the decision as well as the second after that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So: "The Crisis Staff issues the following decision: "All executive posts, posts involving a likely flow of information ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Just read it, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... posts involving the protection of public property, that is, all posts of importance to the functioning of the economy may only be held by personnel of Serbian nationality."

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Would you now please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "These posts may not be held by employees of Serbian nationality who have not confirmed that at the plebiscite or who in their minds are not yet ideologically clear that the Serbian Democratic Party is the sole representative of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please also read the order of Mr. Zupljanin in relation to employees that need to be removed from places where they are not welcome. In the first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, the witness is reading the documents. What is the question? We're coming back to yesterday's question. You have the document. Could you put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me? Can you hear me, Mr. Simic? No? Can you hear me, Mr. Simic? Is there a problem with the microphones of the B/C/S booth? I see the microphones are on. Can you hear me? Perhaps it's a problem with the channel for Mr. Simic. Are you hearing now? No? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now. We can hear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine now. In any event, something went wrong and was corrected, so we have to bear this in mind to avoid it happening again. What I was saying, Mr. Simic, was the witness is reading the document but you are not putting questions to him. What are your questions? So I think it's preferable to produce the document and then put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you are familiar with this document. Has Mr. Zupljanin ordered that such persons cannot be dismissed but must be retained in the police system?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the order says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does the date of this order coincide with the beginning of your work again?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was issued on the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, was it regular practice for the chief of the CSB to call police chiefs before making a decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were so-called collegiate meetings. These were quite frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need the document any more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You just said that on the 1st of July, 1992 you were assigned to Tukovi, where you went to work. My question is, so as to avoid three questions: The command structure of the reserve police station at Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander was Mile Drazic, the deputy, Slavko Antonic, and the assistant, Lazo or Lazar Basrak. Some people called him Lazo; others, Lazar.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, my learned friend showed you an order from 1991 on target shooting, signed by the Chief of the Public Security Station, Hasan Talundzic. My question is: The process of target training, is that regulated by the Rules of Service of the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: How is it regulated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a universal rule for target training which is applied in the army, in the Territorial Defence, in the police, in the civil defence, in so-called premilitary training for students at universities and secondary schools, and even during sports contests with rifles. So these are universal rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This type of exercise, is it carried out pursuant to the orders of the appropriate superior?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is he obliged, in his order, to observe these general rules for all the persons participating in the training?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whoever gives orders for such target training with live ammunition is duty-bound to provide for all the other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, we have, quite a number of times, seen Mr. Drljaca's order of the 31st of May, and also the daily schedule issued by Mr. Kadiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could documents D17/1 and 3/186 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I take a moment to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I inform the Chamber, please, that D17/1 is Prosecution Exhibit 2/4.11. It has been referred to fairly consistently in the course of the Kvocka examination under that -- with the Kvocka witnesses under that particular exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Not the B/C version. Not the B/C version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Susan Somers, but we have this problem where we have documents that have two numbers, the same document with two different numbers. We are now separating the documents that have already been tendered by the Prosecution so as to avoid having the same documents marked in two different ways. In any event, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, will you please look at the daily schedule for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 18th of May, 1991. Without wasting time, please look at Mr. Drljaca's order, dated the 31st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do both these orders contain instructions about security?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they both contain instructions of that kind. We spoke yesterday about document -- order number 480 --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is there another number?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there's another. Order number 417. I was focusing on the one under which my name is included.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: So Simo Drljaca's order, does it contain similar instructions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under paragraph 6, "Security services shall be provided by ..." that is the same order, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: If we go back to Mr. Kadiric's order, the work schedule for the 18th of May, 1992, we see that Mr. Kadiric authorised the commander to assign those five men.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Because of the transcript, I'm going to repeat the question, so please answer it once again. In the daily work schedule issued by Mr. Kadiric, dated the 18th of May, for the Omarska Police Station Department, it says, "Five policemen." You told us there were five policemen who could be assigned, according to the plan, by the department commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I'm sorry for interrupting you, but when you say "in this order," when you use the document, could you tell us the number of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is document 3/186.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, whenever you mention a document, mention its number, because that will facilitate our work later on. If we have a number here, then we can find it easily. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Will you now look at paragraph 6 in Exhibit D17/1.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does this order contain a plan for providing security?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a plan of work, the plan for the entire Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, has the usher got this document to place it under the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we having the same problem again? Please do whatever you did a moment ago to repair the problem. You're hearing now?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can hear you, but not the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 17/1, D17/1, that needs to be placed on the ELMO; is that right, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Please put paragraph 6 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: This order, does it also authorise the department commander to assign policemen among those five that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An order has been given and further elaborated. The order is given as to what shall be done and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, when you say an order was given as to what should be done, does that apply to the point when you took over the defined guard posts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That implies that until then, everything had already been carried out as ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you told us that you were an experienced policeman. You have two documents before you. Will you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can remove those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the differences between these two documents, that is, document D17/1 and 3/186, from the standpoint of the service in which you were employed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the security -- regarding the security segment, there is absolutely no difference. The document dated the 18th of May is one in which the station commander issues instructions because only the employees from that station are included. In view of this other order, since some other services from the public security area are included, such an order could not be issued by the station commander as in the order of the 31st of May. Orders are issued to others as well, like the crime service and even the mine management. So the chief of the public security station, in those days Simo Drljaca, was the only one who could issue the order as he was issuing orders to both the crime service and the police. Since I see that he has issued an order to the mine management as well and some others, I can't remember just now the addressees of this order --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the army as well.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to certain military units as well. He did so because he was a member of the Crisis Staff. And it was stated at the top of the order that he was issuing that order pursuant to a conclusion of the Crisis Staff. And being a member of the Crisis Staff, he acquired even greater authority than he would have within the public security system.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, yesterday during your cross-examination, you stated that for the first time in your life as a policeman -- that you handcuffed somebody for the first time in your life as a policeman in 1994. What was the reason for that handcuffing and when was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the end of the spring, if my memory serves me right. There was a series of murders in the town of Prijedor of individuals of Muslim ethnicity. In one of the documents here, a document which was submitted by an expert witness, Sophie Greve, I think she was the one who mentioned that particular incident, and I read about it in that document. At the beginning of June or maybe in mid-June 1994, a team of inspectors from the Ministry of the Interior, from Bijeljina, arrived. The seat of the Ministry was in Bijeljina at the time. And according to what I thought, according to what I believe was happening, they actually placed the station, police station in Prijedor -- they sidelined the police station in Prijedor and took over as regards the investigation of these murders. Zivko Bojic which was a member of the crime section within the Ministry of the Interior appeared, and he requested my superiors that for the purposes of taking into custody the suspects for those murders, which means that they already had some information to that effect, that he should assign me, together with several others, to carry out that particular task. I think the then chief Bogdan Delic was able to cooperate with them, whereas other services in Prijedor were simply sidelined by them. I was the one who received the task, and together with Ratko Kecan, and Prvoslav Sekulic, I carried out that assignment. I don't remember other policemen who worked with me on the case. We took into custody over 20 individuals of Serb ethnicity from the municipality of Prijedor within one week. They were the suspects. They were processed at the time. Some of them were released and sent home. Those -- that was the tactics of the crime department. Some of them were later on taken to Banja Luka, to the investigation prison. We were very successful in carrying out that assignment, according to the assessment by Zivko Bojic and Bogdan Delic, because we managed to take into custody all of them. I remember at least ten of them at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, did -- were all of the victims in these murder cases members of the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost 100 per cent sure that all of them were Muslims. It was a very big case. There was a lot of talk about it, and I never heard that there was a Serb victim amongst them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn why you were chosen by Mr. Bojic from the Ministry of the Interior? Why did he choose you to conduct the detention, the process of taking into custody people who were suspected of having committed murders of individuals of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, I think that he heard -- he said that he had heard about a very dutiful and diligent policeman within that centre and that he thought that he could rely on that police officer for that kind of job because some of the suspects were also members of the reserve police. So I was supposed to take into custody people who were my ex-colleagues or people who were refugees and had come to Prijedor from elsewhere and had to kill the owner of the house in which they were supposed to be accommodated. So it was a very complex and difficult job. From the professional aspect, it was very hard because they were all carrying weapons, but it was also difficult because of the general atmosphere and the environment because people started talking about the fact that we started arresting Serbs as well. The situation was rather complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was that a dangerous assignment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, they were all armed. And later during the investigation, I heard that many of them had indeed perpetrated those acts, some such acts. So they were all armed, and some were murderers. So I don't think that there's anything else that I have to tell you about how dangerous it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You testified that in 1994 you became the shift leader in the general police station in Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the Minister who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Zivko Rakic, that that was the name of that Minister. During those three or four years, there were very frequent changes of the post, but I believe that Zivko Rakic was Minister at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: It's not very important anyway. How did you become shift leader, in view of the fact that up until that time, you had been a simple patrol sector chief and you had been involved in the most ordinary, the simplest tasks when it comes to the overall police structure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must know that sometime in 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Counsel is testifying, and I would ask the Chamber to ask to at least have the question rephrased so that the witness can indicate what the nature of his tasks were, not counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. We always come back to one and the same issue. Please refrain from making conclusions and expressing your opinions here. Try to ask a simple question. What I can read here from the record is the following -- I have to read it in English because I don't have a transcript in French. [In English] "You had been involved in the most ordinary, the simplest tasks." It's an opinion. "And you had been involved in the most ordinary, ordinary, the simplest tasks." Always it's an opinion. It's an evaluation. "When it comes to the overall police structure." So you have to put the question asking, "What were the tasks you did before and what are the tasks you are doing now?" If not, you are testifying on behalf of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, I have to comment. I wasn't making any conclusions. I simply stated what Mr. Kvocka said yesterday and what is contained in the document which has been provided to me by my learned colleague, where it is clearly stated that those tasks were the simplest tasks. It's the rules of service, Exhibit number 3/206. But I accept your suggestion and I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. You're quite right, but it's almost one and the same thing as using the expression such as "war criminals" in some other document that we have seen here. If the document states "simple tasks," then it has to be properly translated and quoted. Otherwise, we risk making conclusions which we do not want to do. Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will accept your suggestion and rephrase my question in order to speed matters up.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what changed? What made it possible for you to be appointed to the position of a shift leader?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to explain this in some detail. In 1993, end of 1993, in the area of Prijedor municipality, a lot of things started to change. Simo Drljaca, for political reasons, was replaced. The new chief arrived; it was Bogdan Delic, but I'm not sure about the exact dates. After his arrival, the arrival of Bogdan Delic, one could feel winds of change blowing in the police service. There was more professionalism, and requests to that effect were being made, which was not necessary in my case because I was a professional, experienced policeman. One of such cases was also that one, because Zivko Bojic, when he came back from the Ministry, he made an assessment of my work, and Bogdan Delic, who was the chief at that time, saw that for himself. In the next organisation of the work of the service, there was a decision made whereby I was appointed to the position of the shift leader at the Police Station Prijedor 1. That was a new police station, because we also had at that time Police Station Prijedor 2 which was established. Prijedor 2 was established in the neighbourhood of Urije, and Prijedor 1, in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kvocka, you, as well as many other witnesses, testified about the time when Mr. Meakic was in the investigation centre. Can you tell the Chamber how much time Mr. Meakic spent in the investigation centre on a daily basis, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there every day. Very often he would spend the night in the centre. When he was absent, he was absent for a couple of hours. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Sometimes he told me that he would go to Prijedor; sometimes he didn't tell me anything about where he was going. I told you about that, and I also told you about what he would usually say, that in his absence I should be there. But he was there every day and almost every night. Witnesses have testified also that he slept there somewhere, but I don't know exactly where it was because I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you said yesterday, and Ms. Somers also referred to an incident with serious consequences. Could you tell us, could you be more specific in terms of the time when the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day of the attack on Prijedor, that is, on the 30th of May. Later on that day, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Could you tell us what incident you're talking about? You just said "to an incident with serious consequences." Just refer us to what specific incident it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The incident which was testified about by witnesses, the shooting incident where three individuals were killed and four were wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald, for intervening in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: My last question for you, Mr. Kvocka: You were at the investigations centre. You have received the documentation which was inaccessible to us. You have heard a number of testimonies about it. At the end of your testimony here, as far as the Defence is concerned, could you tell us who the commander or the warden was and also who the deputy commander or the deputy warden was of the camp or the investigations centre of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documentation which was seized after the indictment was issued, many things became clear, if you want my opinion about that, and it became obvious who was issuing orders to whom. On the other hand, you have the report which was composed by a very qualified commission, including Bera Vojin, the Chief of Security Service from Banja Luka, and also Rajko Mijic, the coordinator who was well-versed in the circumstances and the situation in which the investigations centre was functioning. According to that report, they did not manage to find, to identify, that individual. Moreover, the same commission established that in Sanski Most, it was the Crisis Staff that appointed the prison commander to his post --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the objection that I will interpose is that the witness is not testifying from firsthand knowledge at all, by his own admission, and the value of this, I think, is very questionable. This is an opinion based on a reading of documents, and the question posed was, "Who was the commander of the camp?" He obviously cannot tell you from his own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to reply, Your Honour, to the objection. My learned colleague, in at least 60 per cent of her cross-examination, asked Mr. Kvocka for his opinion about various matters, and the same was the case with the interview of Mr. Reid. We have heard that Mr. Kvocka was a policeman and that he was familiar with the evidence that has been tendered. Why wouldn't he be able to provide us with his opinion? Because he was there, he has heard the evidence, and he can give us his opinion. I'm not asking for anything more than what was amply used by my learned colleague during her cross-examination. Very often she would begin questions with, "What do you think?" or "What is your opinion?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you wish to reply, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you very much. Your Honour, the indictment proceeds from the position of the Prosecution, at the minimum de facto, and very possibly de jure, deputy camp commander status or the functional equivalent thereof. The issues of professional action - "How did you view this? How did you view that?" - was actions committed by this individual. The issue here is an opinion on documentation. To ask him, "How did you view this which you did? Tell us about this," it was referring, if I understand what counsel is saying, to things that he did. How did he view this? Situations in which he was personally involved. What is happening, as I see the response that is coming forth, is it is passing judgement on documentation over which he has no firsthand knowledge, and I think they are very different situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, the Chamber will allow the witness to continue expressing himself. Because he said, "At that time, I was not aware of those documents, and now that I have access to those documents, I have to say the following," the Chamber believes that it is a very important piece of information and that we need to hear it. The objection is, therefore, overruled. Mr. Simic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In order to follow the record easily, we are talking about document D38/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where was I? Okay. So from those documents, it is obvious, as I said, that highly qualified professionals took part in that work --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, sorry to interrupt you. I just need some information. At that period of time, you were not familiar with those documents?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with this particular report. I only received it here during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So from that document, one can see that highly qualified operations officers established that it was the Crisis Staff in Sanski Most that appointed the warden of the prison and his deputy. However, as regards the municipality of Prijedor, that individual was not identified, that is, who was appointed either by the Crisis Staff or some other body. What they established was that there was a system which was in place, in view of the orders and the overall structure; that a system of reporting also existed; that the person who issued various orders was also established, and that that individual established responsibilities for various sectors. It was also established that those people from those sectors were duty-bound to report to him on a daily basis. From two documents, it also can be seen that that individual, that is, the Chief of Public Security Station of Prijedor, on two occasions - we have those documents at this point - that he informed the Crisis Staff. One was an order to prohibit the release, and he issued a follow-up order to the effect that the first one should be strictly respected and obeyed. As regards any further chain of command, I really cannot tell you anything about it. I don't have any knowledge about that and I cannot make any conclusions on the basis of the documents. Everything finished, as far as I'm concerned, with the Chief of Public Security Station. And also I know that he informed and he reported to the Crisis Staff. That is all I know. I know also that the chief was also a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, let me ask you something. Is that all that you have to say, having seen the documents? But forget the documents for a moment. Come back to your presence in the camp. What was it that you yourself perceived or observed regarding the camp structure? Who was the commander and so on? Do you understand my question? Forget the documents for a moment and place yourself in the place and in the time we're talking about and tell us what was your perception of things. What were your conclusions in relation to the camp structure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to do that, Your Honour. Let me start from the place that I'm most familiar with. The only superior to us policemen was Zeljko Meakic, our immediate superior who was there. He was not the only one but our immediate superior. And according to my perception and observations, he could draw up the work schedule for the policemen. He could give them specific assignments. I also noticed this Babic who was mentioned here, but there were other engineers too who worked in two or three shifts, and their workers referred to them as mine managers, as the managers of the mine. And I noticed that they were superior to their staff, that is, the staff of the mine, all the other workers ranging from the cleaning ladies to the maintenance workers. That was the other segment. Within the camp, in the course of my work, I noticed that there were three inspectors or chiefs who were superior to the investigators, and they gave them assignments, but they could also give assignments to the policemen, especially those who were designated to serve them, in a sense. They were part of the duty service. And they could also give them specific assignments, as could the inspectors themselves. So there were three chiefs of those services which belonged to the state, public, and military security services. I didn't notice any other chains of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question based on your observations, if you can answer it. How could Zeljko Meakic organise himself to be at the same time in charge of the Omarska Police Station department and in charge of the Omarska centre? Do you understand my question? Because after all, you have told us that Zeljko Meakic spent most of his time in the Omarska centre. What happened to the police station department in Omarska then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that when the investigations centre started operating, almost the entire department staff was transferred to the camp. There was only one or two policemen on duty in the department and there was a connection to the camp. And should there be a problem, then Zeljko Meakic could give orders from the investigation centre itself. I mentioned yesterday that I went two or three times to intervene on the ground. So there were very few people left. There was just one or two officers on duty. The patrols were reduced to a minimum, and they went out only when a problem arose. So one could say that the police department itself hardly functioned at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue, Mr. Simic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: In answering His Honour President Rodrigues, let me ask you, was there a military segment within the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday when we were reading the list and somebody made a list of ID cards for passes to be issued at the request of Zeljko Meakic, I think there were 18 or 19 people on that list, they belonged to a unit of Territorial Defence which were attached to the police workers to help out in providing security. I think I explained that a little yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let me just add: Did they have a superior themselves?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did have one, but I didn't notice him coming there, and I don't know who he was. But I think that they were given assignments beforehand. Now, whether Zeljko agreed with that superior, as to how they would work, I don't know, but they were given guard posts and, afterwards, they just took up their positions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: We heard here your testimony and the testimony of others about a period when a special unit was there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We repeated that several times. There were two groups that spent about seven days each, until the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they have their superiors that you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned the day before yesterday a name. The superior was Maric, of the first group, and the other one was Strazivuk. I said, "Lukic." It should be Maric. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, were you ever able to see that Mr. Meakic, as the Commander of the police station department, issuing any order to the other superiors that you have listed just now, the investigators, the special unit members, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is well known from before, the chains of work and command differ. After all, an inspector is at a higher level, not to mention special unit members. It is out of the question that orders could be given to them and particularly not to their superiors, also to the mine managers. They had very specific tasks of their own. This was not possible in theory, nor did it happen in practice, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that Mr. Meakic reported about the work of the security? Did he submit any reports about security?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only make assumptions. I didn't see him do it, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And my final question now. When you mentioned the individual who ordered everything and who ordered reports to be sent to him not later than 12.00, who was that person?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the public security station, Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Mr. Nikolic, do you have any additional questions? No? Mr. Fila? No. Mr. Masic? No. Mr. Stojanovic? No questions either because your client was not mentioned. As you know, we have allowed additional questions outside the scope of the cross-examination, just as the cross-examination went beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief. Consequently, it is possible that in these additional questions, matters were raised as new issues. So I'm going to ask Ms. Susan Somers whether she has any questions. Specifically the Chamber noticed, for instance, this question of handcuffing, which was elaborated at some length. So I don't know if you have any questions about it. Following on to what I said yesterday, we have to maintain the equality of arms and always the possibility of challenging points. So Ms. Susan Somers, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the handcuffing, Your Honour, I do not. I would ask perhaps one question about the habit of reading orders and keeping current on chain of command issues, if I may, that would have been linked to the comments on some of the documents from Prijedor. If I may, one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, do you object to such a question being put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid I don't understand what Ms. Somers wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, will you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like, if the Chamber permits me, to ask a question concerning familiarity, regularity, and familiarising oneself with orders that come down, that had come down from either the Crisis Staff or other higher levels in the policing chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this question was not opened here at all, and Mr. Kvocka said very well that he saw all these documents in the process of disclosure. So he has already provided the answer that as a policeman, at the first level he would not have access to those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never mind. We'll allow that question, and if you have an additional question after that, we'll give you a chance to put it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So you have the floor, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in taking up your responsibilities during the wartime situation in Omarska, both the police station and its transfer being into the camp, its appearance as the principal police body in Omarska camp, did you regularly seek, either on your own initiative or during briefings with Zeljko Meakic, to know what was coming down from the political beings in the ARK or in Prijedor itself? Did you stay current with the orders from above?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never had any information about orders except some information that Zeljko Meakic may pass on in the form of his order, because when he would return from Prijedor, he would say, for instance, "Simo told me that information is leaking." And he wouldn't say that to me, he would say that to all of us policemen on duty or on guard duty. "So don't let me see any one of you talking to the detainees." Zeljko would be prone to say such a thing. And also to give a better impression, he would say, "Simo tells me that information is leaking." So he would say something like that. I can't think of anything else to tell you as an illustration of what I mean. So that would be the order he would give us policemen. And it was not part of my duty to inquire about orders. I am very aware of what my duties were as a duty officer in security, as a police officer providing security, and all the other activities of a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You had indicated - this is part of this line of questioning - you had indicated both to Investigator Reid, and I believe you conceded in court, that the Omarska Police Station had resumed its structure which would have authorised a deputy and an assistant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I'll give you the floor later.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. This is for the third time that you are putting that in my mouth. I told Mr. Reid about a theory that existed before the war and was adjusted to the system at the time should an aggression occur. I said that that never happened. Everything changed. All those theories fell apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kvocka, that is sufficient. We know all that. Have you finished, Ms. Susan Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: About the issue of Crisis Staff, you indicated to Mr. Simic that Drljaca was giving this order as a person representing the Crisis Staff. Now, may I ask you, item 17, the final paragraph, says: "The implementation of this order shall be supervised by Police Chief Dusan Jankovic in collaboration with the Banja Luka Security Services Centre and with the support of authorised executive personnel." Do you see any mention of Jankovic's, if any, affiliation with the Crisis Staff, or do you see the Crisis Staff mentioned at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff is mentioned at the beginning of that order, where Simo Drljaca says, "Pursuant to the decision of the Crisis Staff, I order the following." That is the link between the Crisis Staff and Simo Drljaca. The members of the Crisis Staff were various leaders in various institutions in various areas. So that is the link. This last paragraph is his designation of somebody who would implement all that into practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, is it not correct that a superior police officer such as Drljaca could not issue an order that would be inconsistent with a political body known as the Crisis Staff and, therefore, a police order, issued by a police official at the level of Drljaca, would have to be consistent with Crisis Staff decisions. Do you find that strange?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't understood you properly. He is issuing an order on the basis of a decision of the Crisis Staff. Therefore, one can assume that the Crisis Staff took some general decisions, for instance, to arrest people, to take care of refugees, to do this or that, and then, on the basis of such a decision, Mr. Drljaca issues an order. So he was authorised by the Crisis Staff for this segment, the segment of the police activities - that is my impression - the whole police, not just uniformed police. When I say "the police," I mean the whole service; the crime service and the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Ms. Susan Somers, will you finish, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for one more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you have absolutely no idea what decision of the Crisis Staff Drljaca is referring to? Is that not the case, you have no idea?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in that document the number of the decision is referred to. But you have it, you seized that document. It says, "On the basis of the decision of the Crisis Staff." There may be a number there. I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, in reality, did you know what that order was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Ms. Susan Somers, we're turning around in a circle. Mr. Simic, do you have any questions about these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I have none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But remember that we have respected the principle of equality of arms and the adversarial principle. I think that now it's time for a break before the questions of the Judges. I think that Mr. Kvocka needs a rest too; it must be tiring for him. We will have a half-hour break, and I say a half hour based on everybody's watches. All the clocks are showing different times. So half an hour on the basis of your watch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. I have been informed that the clocks have been synchronised so we can have an indication of the exact time now. I will give the floor first to Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kvocka. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'd just like to have a few clarifications from you, and you are the best one, of course, to clarify. Throughout your testimony, I understood that it was a common understanding and rule that no guard should hurt the prisoners and that as a duty officer, you considered it your obligation to report any violation. How many reports did you make? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the number. This was information, but you see there's a problem. Whenever I wanted to inform Zeljko that there were rumours that prisoners were being mistreated, Zeljko almost always responded by saying that he was already aware of that. It was very difficult to obtain information two or three days after the event. You see, these were policemen or guards who hid such information out of solidarity amongst themselves. So that information would reach you with a great deal of delay. It is, however, the obligation of every guard, if he notices another guard doing something wrong, to report it. It is not just an obligation of the duty officer, if I understand your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then let's speak of you as a guard also. What would you do if the violation was committed by somebody superior? We understood that you found it very difficult, but was there any prescribed rule in the system which would allow you to reach higher authorities, to bring to their attention a major violation or a violation which you saw?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To inform Zeljko Meakic, that was the only possibility I had as a guard, as a duty officer, whatever. The only thing I could do was to inform my superior, Zeljko Meakic, even if that person was superior to him. So that's the only possibility I had. But I'm saying again, almost every time he would say he was aware of it, but it was very difficult to get to the root of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. Did you really report to Meakic about every violation you saw? For instance, you saw, as I understood, detainees being beaten going to the toilet. Did you report that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that ever in front of my eyes because if I had, I would have intervened, even though it is risky to do so, as we are colleagues. These are not citizens who are doing it. If it had happened in my presence, I would have intervened. But if I heard subsequently there were such cases, I would inform Zeljko Meakic. And the two or three times I intervened were things that he either saw or was informed about, especially in respect to Djordjin, that incident. So what I'm saying is that that did not happen in front of my very eyes, that kind of mistreatment that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Some witnesses, and I would like to know your opinion about that, some witnesses stated, and we have their names even, that it was inevitable to hear the cries and moans of beatings in the interrogation room because it was on the same floor, I think, where you would be. Whom did you report that to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only time I noticed that I have described, and I said exactly what I did, how I intervened. And I overstepped my authority, in fact, when I acted rather roughly in relation to the inspectors, and they actually complained and said how dared I. That was the only time that I heard it, and I intervened, in view of the limited amount of times I was there, the number of shifts I actually worked there. But I remember that particular occasion. That did indeed happen when I came out of the duty office and acted in a rather rough manner in relation to the inspectors who then complained, what gave me the right to do that, and this had a certain part in the overall negative attitude adopted towards me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that you interfered with them, but what about an official report? Did you give any official report, a follow-up?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did convey the information to Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you stopped at that. You wouldn't pursue it after that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Your responsibility would stop at that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And when Meakic was not there, was there any superior? Did you have any superior?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And your, let's say, jurisdiction covered the whole camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a duty officer in a shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In a shift. For the whole camp? You would walk everywhere?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was my obligation to be in the duty room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because some witnesses, and I would like you to comment about that, some witnesses, I think, saw you walking beside -- you passed by dead people beside the "white house," when you were walking. They said you were walking all over, and they saw you passing by dead people beside the "white house." You yourself said that you saw some dead people. Did you report that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It happened at the very beginning, once when we arrived at work and when we found those dead bodies. And it is an obligation of a police officer to secure the area, first of all, to secure all traces of incident and the bodies themselves. After that, through the duty service, an appropriate report is being made if Zeljko was not there. But Zeljko was there at the time. And the line goes on to the duty service at the police station in Prijedor, which, under normal circumstances, would have to set up an inspection team. But as far as I know, no classical on-site investigation was ever made. The bodies were simply taken to a morgue. Whether anything had been done prior to our arrival, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Once you discovered that such violations were committed, while you were a duty officer, did you take any preventive measures or I won't say orders, but you are the duty officer, you did not inform or warn the guards not to ill-treat the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, it was very difficult to get access to information. Information was always a couple of days late. We would know only a day or two days later that the beating had taken place, so you no longer have a possibility to intervene. An incident had already taken place at the time I heard about it. As a police officer, as a duty officer, whenever I learned about such an incident, I would always report because that is my obligation. Every time I reported of such incidents to Zeljko Meakic, he would tell me, almost all the time, that he knew about it but that he simply couldn't get to the root of the matter. He didn't know where the origin -- what the origin of the incident was. Whether he reported to someone else further on, I don't know. For him to be able to do something concrete, to do something specific, I think that he would have to institute some disciplinary action with an appropriate commission, a disciplinary commission. In view of the fact that I know that two or three guards were dismissed, I can only conclude that he, indeed, achieved some results to that effect, because I know that two or three guards were sacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If I remember rightly, one of the witnesses, in fact, testified to your advantage that the camp atmosphere was better when you were a duty officer. Did you do something about it? Did you do anything, in fact, to alleviate the suffering of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was probably the impression and conclusion of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. detainees as regards the overall atmosphere. But I always tried, because I was familiar with the work of the police and because I had an order to that effect from Zeljko Meakic, to tell those reserve police officers that they should behave themselves. It was difficult for me to lecture them, but Zeljko told me that it would be enough to tell them to just be quiet, to refrain from any contact with the detainees. That was the kind of instruction that I had from Zeljko, and he would repeat that instruction from time to time; that is, he would tell me to remind the prisoners of that occasionally. Because I had two or three interventions of some kind, maybe that created the impression that while I was there, that in my presence, those individuals refrained from such type of behaviour. Those people knew me from before. They knew me as a policeman and they knew that I would probably intervene, so they must have had some kind of respect for me. But that is, of course, their opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the fact, in their opinion, that the guards were nicer to them under you as duty guard?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We had enough evidence that you helped your brothers-in-law as much as you could. Did you help others too? And to what extent, really, did you try to alleviate their suffering?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not ample opportunity for me to act that way. I could have given them a cigarette or two from time to time. I never spared any effort to give them food. But as regards my brothers-in-law, whenever I tried to distance myself from the detainees, because if anyone noticed that I was paying special attention to one of the detainees, then some of the guards, because they were angry or they wanted to avenge themselves, could perhaps then harm the individual in question. They would usually then say -- they would have said, "You are now under Kvocka's protection, but now he is gone." So you had to be very careful, very prudent. I wanted to help as much as I could, but it was very difficult for me to find the appropriate ways of helping the detainees in order to avoid any countereffect of my conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can you really affirm that you never saw a beating and accepted to let it go? You never saw a beating and just stood aside, stood aside? Because some witnesses testified that they were beaten and you were standing against the wall. Would you be helpless and not be able to stop it, as a duty guard?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of how the service was organised, I was helpless. I would have intervened, speaking personally, but there were no such cases that happened before my very eyes, except for the incident that was mentioned by (redacted), when some people were brought there and lined up against the wall, when he wasn't lined up against the wall. It was a very humiliating search, I know that. And also except for these interventions that I do not wish to repeat. But there were no other cases of anyone being beaten before my very eyes. Yesterday, I think I mentioned the incident involving the singing of songs which I could observe from a window. But there was a very large group of military police there and it would have been very difficult for me to do anything. I can claim with full responsibility that nothing happened before my very eyes without my intervening in that; although it was a very risky thing to do because I would have had to intervene in respect of one of my colleagues and not citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Speaking of intervening, would any other guard also have this prerogative to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, of course a colleague is entitled to warn a colleague of this type of behaviour and to prevent it as well. However, in view of the circumstances and the overall tension, it could happen that they helped each other in that, in beatings, for example. That's why I'm saying that it was very difficult to have access to such information, the information about such incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because according to some witnesses, you could order -- for instance, they say that once on their way, two witnesses were going to the "white house," and then you told the person taking them, "Bring them back to me afterwards." Whatever the reason was, you could tell the guards to do that or that, according to this incident, being the duty officer. Is my understanding right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I know what specific event you have in mind, but I cannot remember exactly what happened. However, I know that the military police came on that occasion and called out certain names. They wanted to take those people for interrogation. It is possible that some of them may have inquired about where they were to be taken after the interrogation and that I could have said in passing that they should be returned to the same place as they were initially. They didn't ask me that as a kind of superior officer but as a simple guard. They just wanted to know where the individuals should be taken to after the interrogation. It happened at the beginning when there was a large number of members of the military police there, including their own investigators, because they had investigators of their own and they came at the beginning to ask for some people to be taken for interrogation. But we had our own interrogations which were taking place within the centre, but that was in addition to that. So it may have happened, but I'm just sorry I cannot remember exactly how it went. The principle and the method was the same as in the case of that gentleman who asked whether he was allowed to go to such-and-such room. So wishing to help him, and this is, I believe, what he stated here in his testimony, that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that you are a simple guard, but when Meakic was not there and you were the duty guard, didn't you have the same powers as Meakic, being his representative?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Zeljko was the department commander. There were no other superiors, and he could not be represented by anyone. A duty officer acts in his own capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you were his deputy when he was away.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You have the same responsibilities or is it different in your police system? I mean, in an institution, would a deputy replace his boss in all his authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where such a provision exists. There is not a deputy commander position within a police station department. The duty officer does not have authority to replace the commander. If Zeljko Meakic is absent, then the duty officer can report or convey information further on to his superior, to the chief of -- to the chief of the public security station in Prijedor. The thing is that Zeljko Meakic does not have a deputy. There is no provision for that post within a police station department [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Let's not use any words, but you replaced him, and according to what we heard also from you, that he would confide in you and ask you to be his representative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, the witness is going to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I never said that, nor did that happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry to interrupt you, Judge Riad, but you cannot see, perhaps from where you are, that Mr. Simic is on his feet. Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. There is an error in the transcript. Can we have some clarification as regards the status of the deputy commander? The transcript says that there is no provision for the post of deputy commander, and Mr. Kvocka said that actually in reality, that was not the case either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, after all of the suggestions we had regarding this issue, I talked to the people who are in charge of the transcript, and I have to say once again the transcript is always revised. So what you're getting now is just a provisional version with a delay and no corrections have already been made, but this transcript is going to be reviewed by the court reporters and checked once again. So your intervention in this case has, so to speak, corrected the transcript, but the court reporters will once again, of course, check the transcript and the original. It is true that the transcript is authentic, is the authoritative version, but you have helped us by saying that there has been an error in the transcript. However, I think I will have to ask you at one point in time that you would have to point to the problem in the original language and compare it with the translation. At least that is how I understand the procedure. With your intervention, the appropriate correction has been made, and I think that we can continue. Judge Riad, please proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. Let us not speak about what a deputy is or was. Let's speak about your effective authority when Meakic was not there. You said that you were the duty officer, you had no superior, and some detainees said the atmosphere was better. So would you agree that you were in charge of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how to comment on the impression of other people. When Zeljko was absent, all others were equal, both the guards and the duty officer. Well, it was -- the work of all individual guards is provided for in the rules of service. When Zeljko Meakic was absent, and that didn't happen very often, that is what we heard from all witnesses, witnesses of all -- both parties, all other guards are equal. No one could issue orders to anyone else, nor could the duty officer issue orders to a guard, nor a guard to the duty officer, nor could the guards issue orders to each other. Some guards were better at their jobs and some were perhaps not as good in accomplishing their tasks, so that also affected the overall situation, because we have heard a lot of testimony here and a lot of statements which were not presented by the Prosecution. This was said in respect of many other people, that things were better when so-and-so was on this guard post and things like that. So that is what we're talking about. So it was perfectly logical that when I was on guard duty that I would act in accordance with my moral principles and my professional police expertise and knowledge. It was possible that during that period of time while I was on duty that things were better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So the guards were the same under Meakic and under you as the duty officer. Without giving orders, they had to abide by the code they have, which is, as you said, you should not hurt the prisoners. So they knew that. You would not allow it. Would you accept this conclusion to their statement that the atmosphere was better? Because it was the same guards.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning of the work of the investigation centre, an incident occurred, and I believe I showed some of my professional qualities as a police officer during that incident, which probably gave a certain impression, created a certain impression amongst the guards. They knew that I would prevent them in their misconduct, and they probably knew that I would inform Zeljko about everything that I observed. Their assumption was that I probably would not hide anything, because when they saw what my attitude towards Muslims was, their assumption was I would not hide anything from Zeljko, any information that I come across.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: During your being a duty officer, you said also that you have to ensure the security of the camp with regard to people coming in. Of course, coming out-- of course prisoners running away, but also people coming in. Was it easy for people to come in?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the job of each particular guard, to prevent such entries into the compound. In view of the fact that the duty services performed from an office, it is impossible for a duty officer to do that. However, if a guard behaved himself in accordance with the rules, appropriately, then he would prevent such entries; if he couldn't prevent such entries but wanted to do so, then he would probably call for help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. You yourself were able to stop somebody?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
