utterances.text: Yes, Djordjin, for example, whom I mentioned earlier on. I stopped him because he passed through the guard post. The guard did not react, didn't do his job. I noticed him, and knowing that -- although it was very difficult to tell in such situations whether he was there officially or unofficially, but I happened to know him as a criminal, and I realised that he was drunk, that he was making a lot of noise, cursing, I realised that he was not there on any official business. So as a police officer, I intervened, of course, regardless of the fact that, in accordance with the rules, I would have had to call the military police. But then it would have been too late and he would have already done something. So in order to protect people, sometimes you had to bypass the usual procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you had the authority to do it? As the duty officer, it was your right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a policeman, regardless what position he holds at that particular time, whether he's on duty or a guard at a particular guard post, a policeman can always do that. But as this was a military person, a military officer, the proper procedure would be to inform the military police to deal with it. But by the time the military police arrives, he could have killed ten people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: During this period, were you ever informed that Zigic came into the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There are some testimonies I would like to know your comment about. One concerned the fire hose. Some witnesses, as you must have heard too, they said that the detainees were taken to be bathed with a fire hose and that you were sitting in a chair against the wall and gave Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. orders to the guards about how to wash them, and said things like, "Increase the jet," and that sort of thing. Do you remember something like that, for any purpose?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just remember the testimony about that, but I think that in the cross, it was cleared up. The person was referring to Milojica Kvocka, and it was at a time after I had left Omarska. There was no bathing while I was there in Omarska in that way. I said here that I would notice people washing at the water taps in front of the administration building, from the waist up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And another witness, I'll help to say his name, I don't know if it was -- I won't say it; perhaps it was a closed session. He testified that the guard who was beating him told him that he was instructed by you to kill him and throw him into one of the mine shafts, but the guard changed his mind. Does this remind you of any incident? What's your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that never happened, I'm quite sure of that. If necessary, I can read the solemn declaration again here. Such a thing simply did not exist during my stay there. I think I remember who it was who said it here and why he said it, and again in the cross-examination, it was cleared up that he was referring to a date around St. Peter's Day, a time when I had been working at Tukovi for some time. I remember fires being lit at Tukovi and traffic stopped at the time. So I feel embarrassed to comment on that testimony, but I think it is quite clear. The person who mistreated him was a person who had come from the outside and not a guard, as he said himself, and it was prompted by personal reasons of revenge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, while you were at the camp, did you hear stories, rumours, information, about outsiders coming in and abusing the prisoners? People who were not authorised employees or members of the military or security patrol coming in at night, usually, and abusing the prisoners, did you hear about any of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were stories to that effect among the guards, because at the beginning there was general confusion regarding entry. It was sufficient for someone to be in uniform and to have a military booklet to be able to enter the investigations centre, allegedly on some sort of business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did that situation clear up or get better during the time that you were in the camp, or did it stay during the month of June until you left?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have the impression that there were many or frequent such instances. I heard two or three accounts of that kind, that the military policemen had come to conduct some investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Was any bulletins or lectures made to the guards who were guarding the outside perimeter of the camp by either you or Mr. Meakic in order to try to stop these outsiders from coming in who were abusing the prisoners? Were any steps taken to stop that, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the outside perimeter, if you are referring to the second circle that was referred to here, I believe that Zeljko did not have any contacts with them. As for the guards who were directly posted around the buildings, Zeljko would tell them their tasks every day in a couple of sentences, saying that no one unauthorised should get close to the detainees. He did ask me a couple of times, as the officer on duty, to go to a particular area, and for someone else to go to another part of the camp, to pass on these instructions to the guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: To your knowledge, when he was doing that or when he was requesting that you do it, was reference ever made specifically to the fact that he had heard stories that unauthorised outsiders were coming in and abusing prisoners and he wanted to tell the guards that they should be careful not to let that happen? Did he say something like that or ask you to say something like that to the guards, that "We have heard that some of this has been happening and we want it to stop"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would say that, "It appears that people from the outside are entering without any authority, and I have to tell the guards to try to prevent that, to seek assistance if they are unable to prevent it themselves," he did say things like that. But he didn't explain how he learnt about it. He would just say to a guard, "Be careful. Do not let anyone approach the detainees."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We have heard testimony, and you have been present in the courtroom and heard it too, that sometimes the camp's own guards would call people out, and then those people would be taken elsewhere and when they were brought back they would show signs of being beaten. I'm not talking about into the interrogation; leave that out now. Just at night or other times. My question to you would be: If one guard in the camp came to the hangar or some other place where the prisoners were being kept, called out a prisoner, would the other guard who was guarding the hangar or guarding the other place have to let the first guard take the prisoner away? I mean, would that guard who was in charge of the hangar have any authority to question the guard who came and said, "I want this person to take away"? How would that work? If they were all of an equal status, could one guard say, when someone else said, "I'm here to take this person out," could he say, "Well, by what authority?" or "Where are you going to take him?" or that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. The guard on watch should not allow anyone to approach that place, except for those cases during the daytime when there were interrogations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- then there was a group of guards who could go to any part of the camp. The question now is whether every guard acted as he should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the guards were ever specifically told that their duty was to guard the prisoners in whatever rooms they were guarding and that they had a duty to at least inquire as to the authority of any other guard who came to remove those prisoners? Was that subject ever talked about, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko would sometimes address us with a couple of sentences when we came to work and when we were lined up. He would be angry, he had probably heard something, and then he would say something to the effect, "Don't let anyone interfere with your guard post," something to that effect. He would keep repeating such instructions. "Avoid all contact with detainees, and do not allow anyone to approach the detainees where you are on guard." There were such instructions. When there was a takeover of shifts, we would all be lined up, and he would make such -- give such instructions or orders to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us that, in your view, there were no shift leaders in the camp, that everybody under Meakic was on par with each other, there were not shift leaders. On the other hand, we have had, I would say, dozens of witnesses who were detainees in the camp who did tell us that their view, widely pervasive view, among the detainees is that there were three shift leaders. I think it was Kos, Krkan, Gruban, and Radic. There were four shift leaders. Can you think -- based on your experience at the camp, do you have any explanation for why so many prisoners would believe that the same four people were indeed shift commanders and had some extra authority over and above being police officers, that all the prisoners picked out the same people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I should like to say that there were quite a number of witnesses who, in their earlier statements to the Prosecution, referred to many other people as leaders, like Mico Hrvacanin, like Rajko Marmat, and the Prosecution reduced that number to these four. They didn't produce the others. So these are impressions guided by the work post. The fact that you're in an office puts you apart from the guards visually, and it gives people the impression that you may be doing something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned, I believe, that at the time that the Omarska Police Station took over some responsibility, the question is some or all responsibility for guarding the camp, that you had not only your several active police officers but you had up to something like 65 reserve officers or some large number. Sixty-five may be wrong, but you had a large number of reserve officers coming in. You also mentioned on at least one or maybe several times that some of these, not all but some of these would be new, without a lot of experience, and you even mentioned that some few you thought may have had criminal backgrounds in the past. Now, my question is: Were these reserve officers on a complete par with the active officers once you got to the camp? In other words, if a reserve officer, a new reserve officer was guarding the hangar, would he be fully -- would he have fully as much authority as a much more experienced police officer who might be performing the guarding function in some other part of the camp? I mean, his words, his actions would be given the same weight as a more experienced active officer, and there would be no supervision, nobody could tell him to do or not to do something except Meakic. Is that a proper understanding, and if so, can you give us some idea why that would be good police practice to do it that way, not to have some kind of shift commanders or some kind of intermediary officers who would at least keep some track of such a large number of new people coming to the job for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many questions that I have to answer now. There were newly-admitted reserve officers. Talking about the number, 50 or 60, I always included the 20 that we mentioned today that were helping out as guards. If we're talking about reserve policemen, those who used to be policemen before and those who were newly admitted, they are completely equal in terms of rights and duties with active policemen. These new ones didn't even have a proper ID card, but former policemen had an identical official card as us active policemen. The difference could be noted, however, in the method of work, of course. When talking about shift leaders - I think a part of your question referred to that - that duty officer would be the link between the policeman and the commander, either the immediate superior commander or the police station and a shift leader in Prijedor. So the shift leader in the camp does not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, were you -- you have, I believe, described the functions you were performing in the camp as roughly approximate to those of a duty officer in a regular police station or department; is that right? I mean, I think you've used that as an analogy several times. So you were the duty officer, if I understood your testimony correctly, whenever Meakic -- in the few instances when he was not in the camp. The time when he was not in the camp, you were performing the functions of a duty officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. In a regular police station, in a peacetime police station or a police department, does the position of duty officer rotate or does one person have it all the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They rotate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So this was different in that respect, that you were the only duty officer authorised to be a duty officer when Meakic was not there. That was different from a normal police --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No? Why? Why?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Maybe there's a misunderstanding. I wasn't the only duty officer. In a shift, there would be several duty officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: At the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and otherwise, in a police department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let's talk about the camp now. So you're saying that at the camp, you were a duty officer but there were other duty officers too. Now, were they the same duty officers or was there constant change? And were their functions as duty officers different from your function? You have told us many times that Meakic, when he wasn't there, wanted you to be the duty officer in his place. I'm not saying you were the commander, I'm just saying that when he wasn't there, you were the duty officer. Okay? So when you were that duty officer and he wasn't there, were these other duty officers just duty officers for what purpose? I mean, for part of the camp or a shift or what? I don't understand, because we haven't -- I don't remember reference to them before. How did their functions as duty officers be the same or different from your function as the duty officer when Meakic wasn't around?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All duty officers are equal, and there were three shifts of duty officers, and in principle, they were the same men. There could have been certain changes. So in one shift, you would have as duty officers myself, Radic, and one of these persons I have mentioned. So there could be changes, but because of the shifts and off-duty time, once you enter a certain system of rotation, the same people usually come up again so that in the duty service, there were several duty officers, and in a single shift there were several duties officers. There wasn't just one duty officer per shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But I go back to the fact that I think you have said, both before in the statement, allegedly, of Mr. Reid, and I think here as well that Meakic did say to you, "When I'm gone, I want you to be here and be the duty officer." But if Mr. Radic was also a duty officer at the same time, let's just say it happened to be his time to come up on his shift and so he was a duty officer at the same time, you're saying that you and Mr. Radic would both be duty officers and you would be exactly equal. If something happened and somebody had to report to a duty officer, they could report to either one of you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said, in principle, but probably Zeljko thought if Radic was there, I was not necessary. But if some others were on duty who were not active policemen or who didn't have the same amount of experience or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those he thought would not inform him properly, then he might say that one of those, that number, that circle of policemen would stay when he was not there. So I was talking in general. So it wasn't always that whenever he was not there, I should be there. That wasn't a 100 per cent rule. He tried to achieve that, but it couldn't be done 100 per cent. It was probably his wish to make sure that he would be regularly informed and nothing would be held from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that when you had to return your brothers-in-law to the camp and you did so, you talked to some of your friends, defendant Kos, and you mentioned some others, and asked them, in effect, to keep an eye on your brothers-in-law so that, quote, "something stupid would not happen." Then when asked to elaborate what "something stupid" was, you said, "Well, it could be beatings, it could even be killing." Where would you have expected, from what source, not necessarily an individual to name, but just from what source would you have expected those beatings or possible killings to come, outsiders coming into the camp, guards in the camp, where? What source were you worried about with respect to your brothers-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, because of a certain number of guards with whom I did not get on at all at work and possibly beyond them as well, and in view of the fact that I had heard that there were guards who were inclined to beat, that was the source of my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I have one more specific question and then three very general questions and I'll be through. You told us about two different incidents, one in which you saw, in the early days, prisoners being taken off of the bus and having to go through a cordon, and yesterday you said that involved some slaps and singing of Serbian songs. In the earlier interview with Mr. Reid, when you were asked, "Did you ever see cordons or lines of police and escorts lining up and the prisoners having to pass through?" page 42 of the English, I'm sorry I don't have the B/C/S, but I think you'll remember, "and being beaten while we were passing through," and you said, "I think in the beginning there were situations." "Did you see that?" "Yes, in the beginning, at least once." My only question is: In that instance, you told us that you didn't think it would be wise to intervene. You certainly couldn't use firearms and worry about people getting shot in the process. You also told us about an incident in the early days too in which, I believe, the Banja Luka contingent from the army that was doing security, or some outside army group like that, was searching the prisoners very roughly and you did intervene, you did intervene. I'm wondering if you would tell us why -- and in both cases, you were dealing with people who were outside of the regular camp guards. In the first, you told us that these were the people who escorted the people there, and you thought they had jurisdiction over the prisoners until they actually got accommodated in housing, at which time the regular guards took over. But in both of those cases, you were dealing with outside groups that were in charge of the prisoners. In one, you intervened to try to stop the rough searching; in the other, you decided you wouldn't intervene, it wasn't necessary or wise. Can you tell us why you drew that distinction?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first intervention, I said, consisted, really, of a comment on my part because the superior was nearby and I wanted him to hear it, regarding the search which was not done properly. That is the first incident. I simply couldn't keep quiet so I opened my mouth. But it wasn't too drastic, that is true. In the second case, I saw that they were bringing in people by buses. I saw this through the window, and this took about ten seconds. Get off the bus, running between cordons, and then a slap or two, and then they would shut them up in the garage, which is the first premise from the entrance to the camp facing the administration building. So it didn't last long. You would have to go round the building, and to shoot from a window at a mass of people, at a crowd of people, to stop them singing is something that I really couldn't do. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You have told us on many occasions that if you actually saw an assault on a prisoner, you would, and you did on a few occasions, intervene. But you've also told us that sometimes you would see injuries on prisoners but you wouldn't see any actual assault. You would report that on many occasions to Meakic, but, if I remember your testimony, you never heard or knew of any formal investigation being initiated to find out about any of those things. If that testimony is correct, as I heard it, what, in your mind, would be the solution? I mean, how, in the camp situation, would you ever be able to stop these attacks if you only found out about them later, you reported them to your superior, but apparently nothing was happening? I mean, what, in your own mind, did you think it would take to change the situation? How could it be changed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko should have gone further up and requested a change among the guards from somebody who had the authority to do that, or I don't know myself what other possibilities he had. As for me, seeing that this did not have much effect, because you would hear every four or five days that somebody had been beaten up, and because of all the other reasons I gave, I would get out of the office so that at least my presence might have some effect in stopping it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last two questions. Were you aware, during the month that you were at Omarska camp, that when you looked around at the total situation, at everything that was happening that you could see, everything that you could see, were you aware or did you believe that these prisoners were being held or detained in violation of international humanitarian standards, like the Geneva Convention or any others? Not your responsibility, but that in general they were being held in conditions that were violative of the humanitarian laws.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I take into account the regulations themselves, I believe that they are for sure in accordance with the Conventions, and I can say that they were violated, the regulations, that is. But we couldn't know whether an investigative magistrate had ordered a detention or not. As regards the conditions of the detention, there were probably violations. That could be observed; one could see that the conditions were not such as to justify the treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My very last question, then - and I thank you for your patience - is: If the incident which provoked your leaving the camp had not happened, suppose that just did not happen, and things went along exactly the way they had been going along before the incident with your brothers-in-law came up or any retaliation to you, do you believe that you would have stayed on in the camp until it closed? Would you have continued to serve in the camp until it closed down or until you were assigned some place else?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is that I would have stayed if I hadn't done what I did. However, in view of my methods and my attitude, my conduct, I think that I was a black sheep amongst the guards as well, amongst the administration, the population, that they all considered me to be a black sheep. That is my general opinion of my situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But from your own point of view, you would not have been -- you would not have felt that you had to leave for any reason, for any personal reason of your own?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it's, again, a matter of striking the right balance. In my mind, I was tormented with two possibilities. On the one hand, I wanted to leave and abandon it all; however, when I thought of what could happen if I should leave, I didn't have any possibilities, any future. On the other hand, nothing would happen, nothing would change in the investigations centre. Nobody would gain with my departure. On the other hand, I was also faced with the choice of staying, for all of the reasons I have mentioned here. So that was the kind of struggle that went on in my mind all the time. I wanted to leave it all behind, and on the other hand, I wanted to stay on because, if nothing else, I was willing to help other people. But I was perhaps able to do so only in respect of my friends and relatives who were there. So I was confused. I wanted to leave but I knew that I had no place to leave; I couldn't go further than Banja Luka at that time. Plus the overall situation, the wartime, the front which I would have been sent to if I had left the police. And then I would also leave all my family behind. I didn't know what to do with my wife, with her brothers, with my children. So those were the two options that were conflicting in my mind at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. I hope, Mr. Kvocka, that you still have enough energy to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. To follow up on a question which was asked of you by Madam Judge Wald, it regards your departure. Was it a kind of relief for you or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I did -- it was a kind of relief. But I was also worried about the people who had stayed behind and the people whom I was supposed to take back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been asked a number of questions after your testimony and during your examination in general, but I still have a few questions for the purposes of clarification. You remember the incident involving an individual by the name of Djordjin. You told us at one point in time that you had seen this individual in front of the window of your office. Do you remember when you saw him for the first time? Where was he? Where was this individual?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was approaching the administration building from the direction of the entrance, and if, looking from the window of the duty room, you can see that portion of the road, he had almost reached the building itself. So I think that, as the crow flies, we can talk about a distance of perhaps 20 metres. At that point, I saw him. I saw that he was making noise -- actually, I must have heard the noise before which prompted me to look through the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kvocka. We have spoken about shifts at length here. You have already vigorously contested the notion of shift leaders itself and wanted us to use the term "shift duty officers." Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the title that we used officially, and those who understood the system used that term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, can you tell us your opinion - maybe you have already told us that, but it is very important for us to be clear on this issue - what is the difference, as far as you are concerned, between shift leaders and shift duty officers? I'm sorry that I have to mix French and English, and I know that that confuses the interpreters a little bit. I hope that you will eventually get the translation. Do you see the difference between these two terms? What do you think the difference is?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer, as I have already indicated, is a link between the guards and the commander of the department. The duty officer has to transmit the information he has had access to to the commander of the police station department. That constitutes the task of the duty officer, in addition to what I have already said, that he had to be on duty at the telephone, at the radio, and so on and so forth. As regards shift leaders, they have a wider scope of duties. He is not -- his is not a managerial type of position. He is in charge of drafting a daily schedule which is decided upon by the department commander. As regards the profession itself, his position is supposed to be a more professional one than that of the duty officer because the duty officer must consult the shift leader in the station, and the shift leader has wider authority as regards certain orders that he can issue to police officers. For example, he can call on the radio, he can call a policeman from one particular area and tell him that something is happening in another street, that he should go there and check on what is going on. This is the kind of authority that he has while he's on duty. A shift leader is also the one who is to inform the inspection team of the necessity to go and conduct an on-site investigation in case of, for example, traffic accidents. He is the one who has to call the inspector on duty, to gather the team and to dispatch them on the site of the incident. He is also the one who dispatches patrols in cases of intervention. He has wider authority in terms of command as well, although his position is not to be considered a managerial position. He is the one who is doing the work schedule for that day. There is a difference. It's very difficult to measure it, but there is a big difference between a shift leader and a duty officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have already spoken about you, Mr. Mladjo Radic, Mr. Kos, and Marmat being in the same category while you were talking about the duty service, but you know that the witnesses that have testified here and that you yourself have heard have given us an impression that Mr. Radic was there on a given place with his rifle, that he was watching, observing the situation, and as regards Mr. Kvocka, they said that he was from time to time moving around but that he would be in his office most of the time. The impression that the witnesses have given us, does it have some kind of justification as far as you are concerned? Was there really such a difference in accordance with what the witnesses have told us or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their impression is partly justified. However, I must say once again that we all used one and the same duty room, all of us duty officers. There were no other rooms like that. That was the only duty room. So the very fact that the duty officer was there in his room, he was not on guard. If on his own he should leave the room and talk to a guard, that I can agree perhaps gives an impression of difference of work Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the individual did. Now you have to see who was more prominent in that. We have heard testimony that Rade Ritan was some kind of leader, some kind of chief. Neso Janjic, for example. I remember a statement to that effect. I don't know whether it was entered in the record, but to some witnesses, Neso Janjic appeared to be a chief. So in respect of some people, some witnesses said that they were chiefs or leaders or some kind of bosses, shift leaders also. So I can agree with you that perhaps such an impression could be created, in particular in cases of those people who are not familiar with the work of the police and the kind of tasks that the police had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've a very simple question now for you, Mr. Kvocka, and I will have to take an example involving my colleagues. I apologise for that. You can see here that the Judges are equal when you look at the Bench, but who are you looking at at this point?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am looking at you, Your Honour, because you are seeking at this moment. You're sitting in the middle, so that creates some kind of impression as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is that impression?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my impression is that you are in charge. You are conducting proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So one can perhaps conclude that I am more equal than the others, because according to the Statute, all judges are equal. I think your Defence counsel, Mr. Simic, can explain this to you later on. According to the Statute, all judges are equal. However, there is an impression that's created here that I am somewhat more equal than others in this case. So can we envisage a possibility in the Rules and also on the ground in how things actually stood -- so can we envisage the possibility of having one situation prescribed for in the Rules and one situation that was actually taking place on the ground, in practice?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible to envisage all kinds of situations. One can perhaps think of the possibility of someone having authority under the rule but not actually exercising that authority in practice. It is also possible to think of an individual doing his job very well and taking active part in it and also to have another individual who, according to the rules, might be even higher up in the chain of command not doing that, not behaving in that way. So one can draw different conclusions on the basis of that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One other question, Mr. Kvocka. Do you have any indication which would permit you to conclude that you were not a deputy to Meakic and, theoretically speaking, you did not have a possibility to be an assistant either. However, do you have any indication as to the fact that the detainees might have perceived you as having some kind of authority that would have been superior to other guards although, theoretically speaking, you were equal with others? Does anything make you think or conclude that they might think that you were different from others?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they might have on the basis of my conduct in my work, on the basis of the fact that I respected rules and on the basis of their wish to be in my presence and because of the fact that they felt more safe in my presence. So certain conclusions could have been drawn on the basis of that. It was not my ambition to hide anywhere. I made myself visible. Everything that I did, I did in public and it could be observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take an example, Mr. Kvocka. Were you ever with a colleague or several colleagues and a detainee came to talk about a certain problem, and did he ever in such a case choose you to address himself to in order to solve that problem?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the people that I knew, some of the detainees, would address themselves to me and not to my colleague, especially if that colleague was a reserve police officer, and if they had any negative experience with that other policeman, other guard, then they would address themselves to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have told us about an incident, that is, an event when you distributed cigarettes belonging to detainees. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean belonging to the guards. Yes, I remember that. Zeljko gave me cigarettes which I was supposed to distribute to the guards, and I hid some of those cigarettes and gave them to detainees. That was the event that you refer to, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to know whether the guards, your colleagues who had cigarettes, also distributed cigarettes to detainees.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them probably did if they had any. There was a shortage of cigarettes at that time. But some probably didn't want to give them away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid I'm taking too much time with my questions, but I have just a few questions left. You have mentioned three types of security service within the camp, security service personnel. Those three types of security personnel, did they have anything to do with territorial borders of jurisdiction? If you remember that incident involving the arrival of prisoners, the prisoners who were under escort, you couldn't approach them. I would like to know in view of that, was there any territorial -- were there any territorial borders applying -- that were assigned to those three types of security personnel? Maybe it's a complicated question, but I believe that you will understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try. If I understand you correctly, if we are talking about the three types of services, state, public, and military security service, they each worked in their respective areas; however, they compiled the results of their work. I know about that because there were three coordinators of those services who work together and exchange information. So their competence was interrogation and further reporting to higher bodies to inform of criminal reports to courts and the prosecutors. As regards the territorial domain, it was possible for them to ask for specific detainees because at the beginning there were no lists of detainees in the camp at all and the interrogations were conducted in order. They would, first of all, ask the guards or the policemen who were at their disposal to call out people from a given room, and then after awhile, after they have established something through their investigation, they would usually ask for a specific individual and then the guards would have problems locating the individual because at the time there were no records whatsoever. So that was what they did, that was their job. Once the interrogation was over, then they would tell the guard where to take the detainee that has just been interrogated; not to mix him up with those who have already been interrogated or those who haven't, but should be separated, and so on and so forth. So those were the kinds of requests that they made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Kvocka. You know that there were times when we gave witnesses the opportunity to say something that hasn't been said, so I'm giving you that opportunity. Is there something that has not been said and that you would like to say now as a witness? It's a difficult question, isn't it, Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. After everything that we've heard and gone through here, it is difficult to find something intelligent to say. I don't think I have glossed over anything important. There may be some detail because our thoughts were led in a particular direction. In any event, I wish to thank you for listening to me over the past few days. I do apologise if I was a bit sharp at times. I will be very happy if I have helped to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having made that contribution, Mr. Kvocka, in the clarification of points and the rendering of justice. I see that Mr. Simic has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the earlier practice that was observed once or twice, I would beg to be allowed to ask a couple of questions regarding a document that was shown in the courtroom twice. I have questions for the witness, of course, not for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That has to do with the questions of the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You have allowed that to happen earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But tell me, so as to allow you to put the question, tell me, what is the question you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My questions are related to the organisation of the Trial Chamber, either in the national system or the system of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that have anything to do with the Statute that I quoted from regarding the equality of Judges, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is not in dispute, but I should like to ask a question regarding the organisation of a Chamber. I think this question was put to the witness as a test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, let us be practical, and I will appeal to your ability to synthesise. I will also give the floor to the Prosecutor. So you have two minutes only. Please go ahead and put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, how many members does a Trial Chamber have?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does a Trial Chamber have a President?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is that specified by the Rules?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does the President have all authority to run the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is the situation the same in our own national courts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, is it your perception, having just acknowledged your views on the structure, that the President has additional responsibilities that the other two Judges may or may not have? Having nothing to do with equality of status as Judges, but simply responsibilities as President of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to talk about understandings or perceptions. My impression would be that those who put more questions and better questions, perhaps, have greater responsibilities or obligations. So it's very difficult for me to reply. I would say that there's probably somebody who has much greater responsibilities and is not seen here at all and who is part of a Chamber and who has the right to make very important decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I can't not make the comment that I think your reluctance to pursue this line of inquiry any further shows great wisdom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I appreciate your observation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm not going to ask Mr. Simic which is the Rule that says that our Judges are equal. It is Rule 17 which says that all Judges are equal [In English] "regardless of dates of election, appointment, age, or period of service." [Interpretation] I saw that Mr. O'Sullivan had something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have a question for the witness, nor to the Bench on how things appear or how they actually function. But I do have a request, given that the Kos Defence case begins on Monday, and the request that we have refers to our filing of February 12th, which is the request for admission of documentary evidence. Your Honours, I believe, have that request in front of you. We would be very grateful if you could give us a decision on that before we commence our presentation of evidence Monday, to provide us some guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do we have any response from the Prosecution yet? We're aware of your filing. Has the Prosecution responded?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We have no objection to the admission. There were some documents as well that were presented earlier last week, and we spoke inter partes about it and have no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But you're indicating to us now that you have no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were just about to clear up that matter, because the Defence told us that they spoke to the Prosecution which had no objections and now that is confirmed. It is true that we, of course, believed what we were told by the Defence, but we were waiting for an opportunity to have it officially confirmed. So, Mr. O'Sullivan or Mr. Nikolic, everything is fine in terms of the beginning of your case on Monday. Perhaps we can work a little longer so we don't have to come back this afternoon. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I can just convey what Mrs. Nikolic has found out from the ground. All the planned witnesses have visas and passports, and today they are leaving Banja Luka at 2.30 to go to Vienna, from Vienna to Amsterdam, and they should be here Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this evening. Therefore, the witnesses will be ready for Monday, at 9.20, to begin to testify before you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Nikolic, that's very good. Let me just check a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Nikolic, everything is fine, as far as you are concerned, for us to be able to begin on Monday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. Ms. Susan Somers, I think you were going to speak about documents. I think that, Mr. Simic and Ms. Susan Somers, you could perhaps delay that a little because otherwise we'll be working late, and at the Status Conference next week, we can address all those matters. So this is simply a practical issue. Either we have a break and come back this afternoon or we can consider the question of the tendering of documents at the Status Conference which we have planned for next week. In that case, we can break without having to come back in the afternoon. Do you agree with that suggestion, Ms. Susan Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as long as I understand that we are continuing, that this effectively will be a continuation of this portion of the Kvocka cross-examination; that I'm not finished with it and that I can, in fact, at least for the record, request that the documents that I have sought to have marked - some of them, not every one of them - would be moved into evidence, yes, that's fine. I just want to make sure that this is effectively a continuation during the Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers, we have often resorted to this. We release the witness, allow him to leave, and then we address that question afterwards. If we need to have the witness present, then that is something else. But as Mr. Kvocka is always here in the courtroom, there is no problem. Are you agreeable, Mr. Simic, with this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour, at least for once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very briefly, could I request that the Status Conference be held during the first three days so that I can leave for Prijedor as soon as possible? Because my case comes after Mr. Kos and Mr. Kos will be through by Wednesday with his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was planning to hold it on Thursday or Friday. But, nevertheless, we could have the Status Conference on Monday or Tuesday so you will be able to leave then. Ms. Susan Somers, have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber would like to tell the Kos Defence that their case will take place on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday. If we carry over into Thursday, the Chamber has other obligations, I think. I don't know whether I may say it, or maybe Madam Judge Wald would like to express herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm a member of the Appeals Chamber on the Jelisic case which is hearing argument on Thursday. So if it goes over till Thursday, unavoidably, I cannot be here, and possibly into Friday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, in that case, the Chamber can sit incomplete, that is, a Bench of two, according to the Rules. This is just by way of information. But as I have said, Rule 15 bis provides for the possibility of two Judges sitting, if that is unavoidable. I think that Judge Fouad Riad asked for the floor, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, the opportunity has passed, but I do wish to say a few words. When we were talking about equalities and about the possibility of some people being more equal, I should just like to point out that there are cases when people are less equal, which are referred to as grey eminencies in French, who could be more powerful than the king. So that, too, can exist, that somebody can hide behind the scenes and pull the strings. That is just a theoretical observation I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a good thought for the weekend, what I would say in my language. It's poetry, I'm afraid, so I apologise. So we will have our weekend and we will meet again here on Monday, at 9.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of February, 2001, at 9.20 a.m.
